sources.title: Las Inundaciones en la Ciudad de México. Problemática y Alternativas de Solución
sources.author: Ramón Domínguez Mora
sources.publisher: Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México, Revista Digital Universitaria
sources.acquisition_outcome: Original publisher HTML opened normally; complete readable article prose supplied. No denial or availability stop.
sources.actually_read: Title, author/date, historical overview, section 1 La situación actual, final considerations and bibliography. Relevant bounded observations concern artificial drainage, pumping and the Gran Canal/Dren General del Valle relation.
sources.limits: Historical engineering analysis as of 2000, not current operations or route-level map correspondence. Figures and cited underlying works were not inspected.

correspondence.component_scope: Selected western opening and northern bend
correspondence.finding: The chosen opening lies on the mapped channel on the northern margin of the Floresta Estadual do Amapá setting. The original depicts the northward rise and eastward bend as the same Vila Nova watercourse. The source river extends farther upstream than the selected opening, so the opening is not declared the natural source.
correspondence.bounded_component_name: Rio Vila Nova ou Anauerapucu (printed IBGE label)

correspondence.component_scope: Traíras to Santa Maria do Vila Nova and Bacuri
correspondence.finding: The selected eastward corridor past Traíras and Santa Maria do Vila Nova, followed by the southern turn through the Bacuri/Bonsucesso setting, corresponds to the continuously depicted Vila Nova. CPRM independently depicts and names this local river corridor. Adjacent mining-area symbols are not treated as a selected reservoir or managed water transfer.

correspondence.component_scope: Piaçacá junction, Camaipi tributary context and fragment seam
correspondence.finding: Both originals show the northwest Vila Nova approach and the distinct northern Piaçacá branch joining the south-running trunk. The western Camaipi do Vila Nova approach is separately depicted farther downstream in the Camaipi/road-crossing setting. The selected fragment seam is in this trunk corridor; neither tributary name is extended over the selected Vila Nova route. This support stops short of resolving the following western passage.
correspondence.bounded_component_name: Rio Vila Nova, with separate Rio Piaçacá and Camaipi do Vila Nova tributaries

correspondence.component_scope: Western lower-fragment passage and return near Anauerapucu
correspondence.finding: IBGE depicts the Vila Nova continuing through Três Irmãos and the Igarapé do Lago-side bend, east of the selected western passage, before turning into the Anauerapucu reach. CPRM also depicts the southern Vila Nova trunk through Camaipi and does not supply a western through-channel; its sheet ends before the complete eastern return. The Santana planning map supplies regional river-boundary context only. No lake, reservoir, managed connector or continuous western watercourse is established that would close the selected passage. The maps do not prove that the selected passage is impossible, but their available content cannot establish it.

correspondence.component_scope: Rejoined lower Vila Nova and actual terminal
correspondence.finding: From the return near Anauerapucu, the selected corridor follows the mapped lower Vila Nova through the Capinzal and Vila Nova settlement settings toward the waters north of Mazagão. The terminal is in the lower Vila Nova/Anauerapucu–Tancredo Neves setting. The wider Matapi confluence, Ilha de Santana channels and Amazonas receiving waters lie farther downstream and are context, not additional selected fragments. This does not support a literal open-sea terminal.
correspondence.bounded_component_name: Rio Vila Nova; IBGE also prints the Anauerapucu reach alias

correspondence.component_scope: Tidal and waterbody scope
correspondence.finding: The REMEA field-study area description explicitly links the Anauerapucu riverine setting and transport to flood/ebb tides; its original figure locates lower Vila Nova separately from Matapi and Amazonas. The read maps show river channels and downstream islands rather than a selected named lake/reservoir. No present-day tidal limit, discharge, water level, managed operation, or reservoir inventory is established.
correspondence.bounded_component_name: Vila Nova lower river and tidal receiving setting

correspondence.component_scope: headward_opening
correspondence.finding: The selected opening lies in the lake complex west and north of Mount Bumpus. The original shows the initial lake arms and nearby stream connections. Neither an individual feeder hydronym nor a definitive natural source is established. This geographic setting alone does not establish the ensuing eastern transfer.

correspondence.component_scope: northern_lake_transfer_and_northeast_reversal
correspondence.finding: The selected succession turns east from the Mount Bumpus lake complex toward the eastern lobed lake, then northeast before its southward descent. The source shows distinct lake margins, intervening contoured terrain and additional southern and eastern lake/channel routes. A continuous aquatic connection joining the actual selected succession was not established at ordinary corridor scale. This is a through-link uncertainty, not a requirement for every modeled vertex to fall on a source channel.

correspondence.component_scope: eastern_descent_and_first_sheet_crossing
correspondence.finding: The eastern descending lake-and-stream corridor includes the narrow north-south lake near the Read Island sheet edge and its south/east connection into the larger lake straddling the Banning Lake western margin. The originals show this local cross-sheet lake approach; no name is established for these waters.

correspondence.component_scope: eastern_large_lake_to_southwestern_small_water_transfer
correspondence.finding: After entering the larger cross-sheet lake, the selection turns south and southwest along the western side of the Banning Lake sheet through a separate small-water succession. The map clearly depicts a southeastern outlet-and-falls corridor from the larger lake toward another lake, together with distinct western lake and stream systems. It does not establish the selected southward transfer into those western waters. The mapped southeastern outlet is not substituted for the selected route.

correspondence.component_scope: middle_border_lake_country
correspondence.finding: Original cartography shows the small lakes and channels leading into the broad lake at the western Banning Lake margin, its adjoining lake country, and the selected southwestward return toward the Read Island sheet. These are bounded geographic observations. A complete continuous selected route through every intervening middle connection was not established.

correspondence.component_scope: southern_lake_country_to_tassijuak_approach
correspondence.finding: The selected southward transfer crosses successive elongated lakes and stream corridors before its westward turn toward the northern Tassijuak Lake arm. Both originals show this lake country, but distinct lake margins, contoured intervals and channels extending east or west leave the complete selected north-to-south succession unestablished. The lower named lake does not supply proof of the upstream links.

correspondence.component_scope: tassijuak_lake_and_westward_outlet
correspondence.finding: The southern westward selection passes through the long northern lake arm and its westward outlet in the Tassijuak Lake setting. Read Island87D prints Tassijuak Lake on the lower connected lake complex; Banning Lake77C map-margin fish-resource comment3 independently within the companion publication identifies Tassijuak Lake. The name is a lake-component identity, not a name for the entire selected river group.

correspondence.component_scope: named_westward_river
correspondence.finding: The original directly labels Tassijuak River on the selected westward stream/lake corridor downstream of the Tassijuak lake country. Connected widenings, narrow reaches and the lower lake are visible. This supports a bounded Tassijuak River component candidate, but does not establish that the unresolved northern and middle components belong to one continuously supported representative system.

correspondence.component_scope: coastal_approach_and_actual_terminal
correspondence.finding: The selected lower approach turns south from the lower lake and then west through the mapped small-lake/stream corridor into Clouston Bay near Rymer Point. Clouston Bay is the actual selected receiving bay in the broader Simpson Bay/Dolphin and Union Strait setting. Nearby Forsyth Bay and other coastal streams are not substituted as the terminal. The historical source includes seasonal/intermittent-water cautions; no surveyed mouth point, present flow state or exact hydronym boundary is asserted.

correspondence.component_scope: Headward opening, eastward passage and northward regional-sheet entry
correspondence.finding: The national original visibly covers the whole opening south of 81°N in the southern Mylius-Erichsen Land bedrock and local ice-margin setting. The selected eastward passage, small southern bend and northward return are all within that original. The regional sheet starts at 81°N and covers the northern end of part 5, overlapping the national coverage. The opening is not assigned to the regional sheet below its neatline. The national map depicts a predominantly exposed-bedrock belt with local ice pockets; no single natural-river label or surveyed channel through the entire opening is established.

correspondence.component_scope: Westward return and northward approach south of Femte Maj Sø
correspondence.finding: The regional original exposes the whole westward return and subsequent northward turn across the yellow-mapped sedimentary/surficial-cover belt and neighboring local ice/rock patches south of the water body labelled Femte Maj Sø. The junctions with both the entry and lake-side passage are visible at ordinary corridor scale. Geological boundaries and dykes are distinguished from watercourse symbols and are not treated as proof of river continuity.

correspondence.component_scope: Femte Maj Sø lake-side passage and northeastern valley continuation
correspondence.finding: The selected northeastward passage follows the mapped Femte Maj Sø lake/shore setting and continues toward the valley east of its northeastern end, amid exposed bedrock and local ice patches. The original covers the full lake-side interval and the transition into the blue-dotted Quaternary-covered valley belt. Femte Maj Sø is a lake-context label, not a representative river name. The selected line and this thematic source do not establish an exact lake inlet, outlet, bank-following course or hydraulic lake connector.
correspondence.name_scope: Distinct geographic context label only, not a representative natural-river name.

correspondence.component_scope: Eastward valley/rock-margin sequence and eastern northward bend
correspondence.finding: All selected small stored parts of the eastward sequence and its tight northern turn are exposed in the same regional original. The corridor includes a blue-dotted Quaternary-covered valley, its bedrock margins, and local ice patches within Mylius-Erichsen Land. The eastern bend leaves the mainly east-west valley setting toward the rock-and-ice belt to its north. No small part or intermediate join is omitted; the visible terrain sequence does not itself prove a connected natural river.

correspondence.component_scope: Northwestward-to-northward continuation across the Jyske Ås setting
correspondence.finding: The regional original covers the entire northern continuation through the mapped bedrock, local ice and nearby Quaternary-covered depressions in the Jyske Ås setting. It does not portray the whole selected line as a single named channel; portions of the modeled passage correspond to rock/ice terrain rather than a clearly traced river. Jyske Ås is retained only as a landform-context label.
correspondence.name_scope: Distinct geographic context label only, not a representative natural-river name.

correspondence.component_scope: Final northward part and actual selected endpoint at Hagen Fjord
correspondence.finding: The final stored part is read through the coastal bedrock/Quaternary-covered valley setting into the water area labelled Hagen Fjord. The actual selected rendered endpoint lies in that fjord setting, beyond the mapped coastal margin at the ordinary source scale; the stored pre-extension endpoint is in the same terminal setting. This is the final selected point, not merely a nearby named fjord or an upstream stop. The original does not establish an ordinary named river mouth or present hydraulic conditions.
correspondence.name_scope: Distinct geographic context label only, not a representative natural-river name.

correspondence.component_scope: Chosen southern opening at San Lorenzo Techalote and San Fernando
correspondence.finding: The Tlaxcala original places the first selected interval beside San Lorenzo Techalote at the San Fernando impoundment, and depicts an intermittent approach north of that waterbody. Hueyotlipan independently labels San Fernando and lists it among the municipality’s perennial waterbodies in its 2010 hydrography table. Neither source establishes the modeled opening as an official river source or makes the whole northern continuation a single natural stream.

correspondence.component_scope: Northward San Fernando approach and Bernales/El Muerto branch choice
correspondence.finding: The enlarged Tlaxcala original shows the intermittent approach north of San Fernando, Bernales at La Magdalena Soltepec, the distinct El Muerto waterbody and El Rosario approach farther east, and several angular surface-aqueduct lines. The selection turns west through the Bernales vicinity rather than following the separately named eastern El Rosario approach. A continuous hydraulic transfer through the chosen San Fernando–Bernales–western infrastructure combination is not established. Nearby El Cementerio and El Muerto labels are not names for the selected river.

correspondence.component_scope: Eastern approach to Laguna San Antonio Atocha
correspondence.finding: The state originals identify Laguna San Antonio Atocha near the Hidalgo–Tlaxcala boundary, with its eastern setting near San José Jiquilpan and northern Mala Yerba approach. The selection crosses the lake’s southern east–west arm. The hydrographic legend distinguishes streams, canals, dams and aqueducts; the angular infrastructure in the eastern approach cannot be treated as a demonstrated natural river connection solely because it is blue on the map. Its role and direction in the selected transfer remain unproved.

correspondence.component_scope: Western Atocha margin, Zotoluca and northward Chimalpa–Acopinalco passage
correspondence.finding: The selection leaves the western Atocha setting around Zotoluca and turns north through the Chimalpa Tlalayote–Acopinalco plain. Original cartography shows separate linear infrastructure, intermittent channel approaches and small waters in this plain. The whole chosen lake-exit and northward connection is not established as one through-flow route. The separately mapped Apan/La Laguna and Mala Yerba settings do not by themselves prove that connection.

correspondence.component_scope: Acopinalco–Irolo–Fray Bernardino de Sahagún–Tepeapulco corridor
correspondence.finding: Overlapping Tlaxcala and Hidalgo views locate the selected northward passage through Irolo and the Fray Bernardino de Sahagún/Tepeapulco setting. Several surface-infrastructure and intermittent-channel branches occur here. No common name or complete positive hydraulic linkage from the southern lake passage through this entire corridor is established. Laguna Tecocomulco, shown northeast of this interval, is a distinct neighboring waterbody and is not a selected lake crossing.

correspondence.component_scope: Westward Tlanalapa join
correspondence.finding: The original Tlanalapa Relieve map depicts a southeastern approach reaching the urban-area channel and continuing west, with a separate northeastern tributary labeled El Jihuingo. Its hydrography table lists El Jihuingo as intermittent and places the municipality in the Río Tezontepec subbasin. The selected east/southeast approach and western continuation can be located at this ordinary corridor scale; the northeastern tributary label is not promoted to the name of the selected approach or entire system. Subbasin membership supplies no missing upstream connection.

correspondence.component_scope: Tepeyahualco–Santa María Aticpac–Villa de Tezontepec–Tepojaco/Tizayuca passage
correspondence.finding: Hidalgo and México originals overlap through the selected westward bends, the Santa María Aticpac/San Bartolomé Actopan setting, the Tezontepec turn and the Tepojaco/Tizayuca approach. The maps show distinct intermittent tributaries, linear water infrastructure and the nearby El Manantial storage setting. No automatic connection through that storage or every selected branch transition is inferred, and the map-footprint overlap does not establish a single named river from Tlanalapa to Zumpango.

correspondence.component_scope: Eastern Zumpango approach and selected turn along the lake’s eastern side
correspondence.finding: Zumpango’s original Relieve map directly labels Las Avenidas de Pachuca on the approach from the east and depicts its curved course beside the urban/lake setting. Its table lists that stream and Sotula separately and identifies Laguna de Zumpango as a perennial waterbody. The selected westward approach, northern turn and southward eastern-side passage are geographically located, but the maps do not establish all of the chosen channel/lake exchanges. Las Avenidas de Pachuca is retained as a bounded source label, not assigned to the full selected corridor or every neighboring bypass.

correspondence.component_scope: Jaltenco–Nextlalpan–Tultepec–Coacalco/Ecatepec managed corridor
correspondence.finding: The México original shows parallel linear hydrographic/infrastructure features through the selected southern passage, distinct from neighboring tributaries and urban boundaries. Domínguez Mora’s 2000 engineering account describes the Gran Canal del Desagüe as an artificial drainage outlet associated with the Tequixquiac tunnel and pumped urban inflows. This independently establishes a managed regional context, not a southward natural-river route for the selection. No tunnel crossing, operating direction or present transfer is inferred from the model line.

correspondence.component_scope: El Caracol storage/works vicinity and actual southern endpoint
correspondence.finding: The México original shows the circular water-storage feature and the Planta de Tratamiento de Agua el Caracol label near the selected lower passage. The selection then continues south into the linear drainage setting and ends before the separately labeled Brazo Derecho Río Churubusco and Laguna Nabor Carrillo waters farther south. The map does not name the actual endpoint as a river mouth or demonstrate its final receiving link. The 2000 account describes Dren General del Valle contributions to the Gran Canal, but does not identify this model endpoint or resolve its chosen local connection.
